William Howard Taft. The twenty-seventh President of the United States, serving from nineteen oh-nine to nineteen thirteen in a single term between two Theodore Roosevelt administrations. Originally hand-picked by Roosevelt as his successor, Taft disappointed Roosevelt by pursuing conservative policies and alienating the President's Progressive wing of the Republican party. Their bitter nineteen twelve split, with Roosevelt running as a third-party candidate on the Bull Moose ticket, fractured the Republican vote and allowed Democrat Woodrow Wilson to win. Despite an unpopular presidency, Taft later served as Chief Justice of the United States from nineteen twenty-one to nineteen thirty, a role that proved his true calling.

Born in Cincinnati, Ohio, Taft trained as a lawyer and judge. He first gained prominence as governor-general of the Philippines following the Spanish-American War, implementing American colonial policy. Theodore Roosevelt, seeking a successor who would continue his policies while limiting executive power, handpicked Taft as the Republican presidential nominee in nineteen oh-eight. Taft won easily, as Roosevelt remained popular.

Taft promised to continue Roosevelt's trust-busting agenda but proved more cautious and legalistic. He filed more antitrust suits than Roosevelt but with less fanfare, earning a reputation for passivity. The firing of conservationist Gifford Pinchot in nineteen oh-nine alienated Progressives who saw it as capitulation to conservative Republicans. The incident symbolized Taft's perceived abandonment of Roosevelt's reform agenda.

Taft's conservative judicial philosophy clashed with Roosevelt's expansive executive power. He opposed Roosevelt's view that the presidency should do whatever was not explicitly forbidden. Roosevelt, disgusted with Taft's presidency, announced his nineteen twelve return to politics. When Taft was renominated, Roosevelt bolted to form the Progressive Party, splitting the Republican vote.

The nineteen twelve three-way race between Taft, Roosevelt, and Woodrow Wilson resulted in Wilson's victory and the Republicans' descent into factionalism. After defeat, Taft moved to Yale Law School. In nineteen twenty-one, President Warren Harding appointed him Chief Justice, a position Taft considered his finest role, where he shaped constitutional jurisprudence for a decade.
